create-edit.title: Improving the most core data management flow in HubSpot's CRM to save admins time, money, and [data] sanity

intro.p1: Solving customer pain points, driving adoption, and reducing internal and external overhead costs by rethinking the way customers create and edit their custom data properties.

context.title: Context.
context.p1: HubSpot's CRM is the core of their product and where customers first build out their HubSpot experience. This made it critical to nail onboarding and data integration from the start.
context.p2: The challenge was offering a robust data creation and management experience that still felt nimble across customers of all sizes. Internal and external feedback told us the existing framework was rigid, redundant, and limited — the opposite of the original goal. It forced customers of all sizes into a single mold and wasn't meeting their needs.

problem.title: The problem.
problem.p1: A spike in customer support tickets around property management, upcoming internal feature kick-offs, and an opportunity to adopt new design standards from the core product team gave us the perfect moment to rethink and rebuild this workflow from the ground up.
problem.p2: This didn't have to be a large undertaking and I could have taken a more incremental approach with smaller wins over time, but we decided to aim higher, because the potential upside for our customers was worth the risk.

challenges.title: Challenges.
challenges.p1a: The wizard pattern was well-established with customers, even if disliked
challenges.p1b: Even with strong negative sentiment in interviews and surveys, we risked running into usability biases like "it just works" or "I don't like change" mentalities that could drive churn. This same resistance is likely why some customers resorted to building their own API-first solutions rather than adopting a WYSIWYG experience that should have been easier to use.
challenges.p2a: As a precaution, scope needed to be pared down more than anticipated
challenges.p2b: This flow generated the building blocks that supported all other features and flows in the CRM for any customer, so if care wasn’t taken, it could’ve had a catastrophic ripple effect.
challenges.p3a: Getting other teams to adopt a new component proved challenging
challenges.p3b: Several other product teams drove traffic to our page or had built their own features pushing property data to our tables. In a product this complex, consistency mattered and deviations weren't ideal. I worked closely with each team to negotiate, adapt our solution to their needs, and build their confidence in adopting our component over their own.
challenges.p4a: Admins are busy and have lives and we should not be encroaching on them
challenges.p4b: Everyone only has a limited amount of time per day to do any number of things, so why would they want to spend hours (or days) doing a task. If the new flow didn't reduce time on task, it wouldn't have been worth releasing until it did.

solving.title: Problem-solving.
solving.p1: After several major iteration rounds and feedback, I went down two paths: a quick creation component (a stripped-down, deployable flow for more common property types) and advanced property management (a richer experience designed for admins).
solving.p2: We took this approach for two reasons: consistency and role-appropriate experience. Guardrails keep property creation uniform across the CRM, while the two-path framework gives admins full control and gives marketers and downstream teams something faster and more focused.
solving.p3: User testing, beta feedback, and input from our stakeholders shaped the final production spec. I worked with a content design partner to polish the details before handing it off to engineering and shifting into QA.

impact.title: Impact.
impact.p1: After a two-week closed beta and a month-long open beta reaching roughly 15% of Pro+ tier customers, we shipped to production in mid-March to a warm reception on r/HubSpot and our customer forums. Post-release surveys and interviews were promising, with CSAT improving and customer sentiment no longer including words like "archaic," "redundant," or "painful."
impact.p2: In the first month after launch, support volume dropped more than 20% week-over-week, climbing to ~35% in the weeks that followed.
impact.p3: Being that this was my first release where I discovered, pitched, prioritized, iterated, and executed end-to-end in my time there, I was really pleased with the framework delivered and the roadmap that was planned for the future.

retro.title: Retro.
retro.p1: No project is without turbulence, and this one was no exception. A few things stood out as areas for growth.
retro.p2: Communication is a force multiplier at the senior IC level. I had autonomy, but autonomy can breed tunnel vision. Midway through, I recalibrated and tightened how I communicated decisions and added more polish to written updates. It kept the team aligned and the project on track.
retro.p3: HubSpot's concurrent brand and product refresh left my design systems partners largely unavailable, which added unplanned time to the timeline. I adapted by scaling back some decisions where I could, and it didn't hurt the outcome.
retro.p4: Stakeholder management was the biggest learning. This was my first large-scale feature at HubSpot, and I would have mapped the stakeholder landscape earlier in the process. Mid-flight is never the right time to be expanding your audience. It's a lesson I carried into every project from then on.
retro.p5: Overall, I was proud of where it landed, but with the one caveat that some forward-looking ideas I had scoped didn't make it to production before I moved on.

1.goalDetail: Rebuild flow with alternative to wizard structure to allow for more flexibility

2.goalDetail: Increase opportunities for self-service and reduce relevant support incidence volume by up to 20% WoW

3.goalDetail: New experience should be prepared for future AI/ML-friendly features and new core features

4.goalDetail: Bring customers that rely on API or imports/exports for data management back to the table

1.resultDetail: Customers responded positively to fewer required actions and clearer indicators for incomplete steps

2.resultDetail: The highest-incidence requests fell sharply after 30 days in production, with customers resolving more on their own. Results held through a 60-day post-mortem

3.resultDetail: The new framework includes planned slots for AI/ML and an upcoming KB feature to help keep customers on task without pulling them out of the experience

4.resultDetail: Scores improved from ~75% to ~78%, and customers who had shifted to workarounds for complex workflows felt more comfortable returning to the first-party experience

formula-editor.title: Introducing a custom formular editor for calculated properties

formula-tester.title: Improving retention and trust with a new calculated formula tester

intro.p1: Customers couldn't validate their work and were going elsewhere, even leaving the platform, so I introduced a solution to build their confidence.

context.title: Context.
context.p1: HubSpot's CRM sits at the core of their product offering and it’s where customers first set up the infrastructure of their HubSpot experience. To make that good first impression, our goal was to have a best-in-class onboarding data onboarding and integration experience.
context.p2: The challenge with this particular workflow was trying to offer a robust data creation and management experience for customers of all sizes while still making it feel nimble. Based on internal and external sentiment, the current framework for creating and managing data properties was rigid, redundant, and limited; basically the antithesis of the original goal.

opportunity.title: Opportunity.
opportunity.//p1: Between the customer support contact volume related to managing properties, some new features we were preparing for internally, and an opportunity to start formally preparing for and adopting some new design standards our core team was working on, we seized on the moment to prioritize exploring and delivering a new core workflow for creating and managing properties.
opportunity.p1: We had enough of a backlog to inform us that customer support was swamped and customers were clearly frustrated with both existing and new features in the workflow. The problem was that this was a serious commitment with potential to not move the needle as much as some other projects we had in our pipeline. With that in mind, our pitch centered on four key goals:

1.goal: Reduce redundancy by exploring a less rigid flow
1.result: New flow doesn’t require redundant actions and is not strictly linear

2.goal: Reduce relevant support volume by a meaningful amount
2.result: Support volume reduced by ~35% WoW (~20% expected)

3.goal: Improve visibility of new property types and additions
3.result: New test and released property types saw nearly doubled adoption rate in first week compared to previous rate

4.goal: Improve UX flexibility for AI and KB helpers to help drive usage of them
4.result: New framework includes content slots for AI/ML and KB inclusions to keep customers on task and doesn’t drive them away

creation.title: Redundant, rigid, and in need of replacement.
creation.//p1: One of the biggest issues with creating properties was the customer’s desire to test properties and verify feasibility before committing to a specific property. This problem skewed more towards the more advanced property types, but even for simple text properties there was a desire to see if what they wanted made sense and was actually doable.

The workflow only really functioned in one direction. The unfortunate part of that decision was if you wanted to change a detail about the property, you would lose all progress that you had made. Even a simple thing like changing the property name required up to three clicks to get back to the details stage.
creation.p1: Even with a robust backlog, I wanted to get a better picture of customer pain by meeting with a cohort of beta customers. After a dozen or so conversations, the same themes kept coming up: the workflow is rigid and doesn't let them accomplish things in one shot, there are too many required hoops even to set up a simple property, and it doesn't drive adoption of new updates that are useful to them.
creation.//p2: With the linear wizard format, that meant jumping through some hoops just to get to the more “playground” aspect and caused a lot of friction for customers.
creation.p2: If a customer had to make even the slightest change, their expectation was to at least persist the information they had already entered.
creation.p3: Going back meant needing to go all the way back. This problem in itself almost became a battle cry based on the number of times it was shared in feedback.
creation.//p3: Then, at the same time, if a customer wanted to go back, that meant losing all of their work because it wouldn’t translated across properties (this had technical limitations in many cases, but for common cases it could be solved).
creation.p4: Sadly, this was even more painful for more complex property types where maybe a customer had spent several minutes trying to create and test a custom formula.
creation.//p4: Going back meant needing to go all the way back. This became a regular headache for most customers.
creation.//p5: By changing the flow to be non-linear and more of a CYOA experience, we could improve upon several things related to this problem.
creation.p5: The management flow was not so far different, but located in a different panel. Even with a change of space, the primary issue for management revolved around scalability and data density.

manage.title: Fixing friction with unity.
manage.//p1: After creating a property there are some actions that some more admin-type customers may want to take, but its not immediately apparent how/where they can take them. On top of that, certain messaging and feedback was limited in how it was being presented because of the small panel that the properties existed in. That same issue also existed for modifying a property like a dropdown/select and trying to test a formula; all were either not doable or difficult to do in the space that customers had to try in.
manage.p1: Creating and managing properties are, for the most part, admin tasks that have a need for efficiency. In talking to our beta customers, the top three terms that they conveyed for any new features were, "make it efficient," "make it flexible," and "make it familiar."
manage.p2: Therefore, my primary objective was to strategize and craft toward a more unified experience with minimal trade-offs in current and future-looking functionality.
manage.//p2: There were other issues at play related to managing properties that fell out of scope for this project (things like core actions, ie, deleting, copying, etc), but by migrating the management experience to the same framework as the new creation experience, it allowed for more flexibility to perform a task and also allowed for more visibility and discovery for problem-solving tasks. It also allowed for down-the-road improvements like integrations, AI/ML augments, and KB helper injection so that customers would gain more clarity in the moment as opposed to being shepherded away for most of those moments.
manage.p3: The old panel left a lot to be desired according to internal and external anecdotes. It was also starting to get crowded with information and began to feel cramped. With more content and features on the way, it needed to change so that it could scale.
manage.p4: The updated experience allowed for more of the free-flow of information and flexibility that our admin customers were craving for some time.

retro.title: Next steps and reflections.
retro.//p1: The delivered experiences were meeting their intended goals as of spring 2024 when we released both apps into beta. We met with and surveyed customers in a closed beta before getting a quick confidence boost from our support team that their volume didn’t increase (closed beta group was too small to measure a significant change WoW, so we only had them focus on targeted feedback from that group). With that, we posted our public beta and received several dozen adoptions in the first couple of days. From there, it grew to over 300 by the end of the following week, and eventually reached about  15% of the customer base in Pro+ tier very soon after that. Our CSAT remained at ~75%+ from initial release day (peaked around 86% at one point) and customer support reported volume on certain topics related to management and creation started to decrease exponentially until we hit our first 20% WoW reduction goal around day 23 of public beta.
retro.p1: My team launched the new create and management experiences into alpha just shortly before Christmas with the goal of launching private beta in the first two weeks of Jan 2024. I had scheduled some interviews in advance with our alpha customers and CSMs for those customers to get preliminary qualitative feedback to present with the quantitative data we collected. Those conversations and dives resulted in no increase in support contact over commonly flagged issues we were trying to solve and pointed to positive sentiment toward our goals of reduced redundancy and increased flexibility.
retro.p2: One of the goals was to keep customers within the HubSpot app to complete their task without having to contact support, so we wanted to foster a bit more self-service into the flow. I emphasized this in the new experiences by both working with our content designers to simplify helper copy within each step and by creating new content slots to highlight KB articles or [in the future] inject an AI tooltip/card to assist with a task.
retro.//p2: At the same time, there were two UX projects happening concurrently while engineering was in the middle of rebuilding the core tech stack for this product area: this framework delivery for creation and management and an encapsulated quick property creation experience for use outside of the admin space. The quick property creation project actually spawned the larger project, funny enough.
retro.//p3: The coalescing projects meant that a lot of planning was needed to deliver properly. One thing I would reflect on for this projects relates to communication. At one point I was on one track of work and unaware of what my engineering partners were working on. We discovered that we were working on opposite projects at one point and that syncing back up to get back on track was going to take at least a week. This all could’ve been alleviated by a one-line clarification in a Slack message. It taught me a lesson about properly setting the table and making sure that each partner in the pod is aligned at the right time.
retro.p3: The other main point of emphasis was to drive adoption of new property types and features that had been released and were on the roadmap. When using the previous create flow, for example, new property types like Calculated Properties and Sync Properties, two of the currently most popular types for SMB+ customers and which also carry a large up-sell opportunity, were being buried down a long 12+ option dropdown list. Now, by removing some of that red tape and exposing them at once, it reduces choice fatigue and makes it easier for customers to be exposed to new types.
retro.p4: After a several week retro and a private beta opt-in over 40%, we found that CS contact dropped ~25% WoW for flagged topics, adoption of the recently updated Calculated Property type steadily increased WoW, and general customer sentiment remained high and never dipped below a CSAT of ~75% (peaking over ~85% for a portion of time).
retro.p5: On a personal reflection, this project was not perfect or without faults. There were some communication hiccups between myself and my engineering and product partners that led to some unnecessary steps being taken to achieve some goals. It also led to the need to pivot high-level design decisions several times due to some unclarified product and engineering handcuffs I was not aware of (things I was still learning in my first year). To try and remedy it, I created a separate process in our team's OS to make design work and artifacts more visible in all the channels we were communicating in and create basically a Figma dashboard for a project to keep status more honest for leadership check-ins and other communications. A one-liner in a Slack message could've alleviated a bit of this pain ahead of time, but it taught me a good lesson about properly setting the table with my partners and making sure we're all properly aligned on a more consistent basis.

customer-profiles.title: Rebuilding Klaviyo's profile view to scale with customer needs, build trust in self-service, and improve how they understand and utilize their own custom data

intro.p1: One of the most central views of the platform had become a hard-to-navigate data dump, so I set out with my team to improve the experience and unlock how our customers actually use it for both support and discovery.

context.title: Context.
context.p1: The profile page is Klaviyo's core view for understanding how any individual customer has interacted with a brand. It's a dense data hub, but customer come to it for two primary reasons: troubleshooting and discovery.
context.p2: The challenge was offering a robust data creation and management experience that still felt nimble across customers of all sizes. Internal and external feedback told us the existing framework was rigid, redundant, and limited — the opposite of the original goal. It forced customers of all sizes into a single mold and wasn't meeting their needs.

problem.title: The problem.
problem.p1: A spike in customer support tickets around property management, upcoming internal feature kick-offs, and an opportunity to adopt new design standards from the core product team gave us the perfect moment to rethink and rebuild this workflow from the ground up.
problem.p2: This didn't have to be a large undertaking and I could have taken a more incremental approach with smaller wins over time, but we decided to aim higher, because the potential upside for our customers was worth the risk.

challenges.title: Challenges
challenges.p1a: As a precaution, scope needed to be pared down more than anticipated
challenges.p1b: This flow generated the building blocks that supported all other features and flows in the CRM for any customer, so if care wasn’t taken, it could’ve had a catastrophic ripple effect.
challenges.p2a: Getting other teams to adopt a new component proved challenging
challenges.p2b: Several other product teams drove traffic to our page or had built their own features pushing property data to our tables. In a product this complex, consistency mattered and deviations weren't ideal. I worked closely with each team to negotiate, adapt our solution to their needs, and build their confidence in adopting our component over their own.
challenges.p3a: The wizard pattern was well-established with customers, even if disliked
challenges.p3b: Even with strong negative sentiment in interviews and surveys, we risked running into usability biases like "it just works" or "I don't like change" mentalities that could drive churn. This same resistance is likely why some customers resorted to building their own API-first solutions rather than adopting a WYSIWYG experience that should have been easier to use.

challenges.p4b: Everyone only has a limited amount of time per day to do any number of things, so why would they want to spend hours (or days) doing a task. If the new flow didn't reduce time on task, it wouldn't have been worth releasing until it did.

solving.title: Problem-solving.
solving.p1: I decided to go down two paths: a quick creation component (a stripped-down, deployable flow for more common property types) and advanced property management (a richer experience designed for admins).
solving.p2: This approach happened for two reasons: to set guardrails that keep property creation consistent across the CRM, and because not every user needs the same experience. Admins get full control and flexibility, while marketers and downstream team members get a faster, more focused experience tailored to their needs.
solving.p3: Signals from user testing, the beta periods, and internal support feedback gave me what I needed to start assembling the final production spec. With help from a content design partner to polish some final details, I handed it off to engineering and shifted into QA to aid them through their sprint.

impact.title: Impact.
impact.p1: After a two-week closed beta and a month-long open beta reaching roughly 15% of Pro+ tier customers, we shipped to production in mid-March to a warm reception on r/HubSpot and our customer forums. Post-release surveys and interviews were promising, with CSAT improving and customer sentiment no longer including words like "archaic," "redundant," or "painful."
impact.p2: In the first month after launch, support volume dropped more than 20% week-over-week, climbing to ~35% in the weeks that followed.
impact.p3: Being that this was my first release where I discovered, pitched, prioritized, iterated, and executed end-to-end in my time there, I was really pleased with the framework delivered and the roadmap that was planned for the future.

retro.title: Retro.
retro.p1: This project wasn't without turbulence. From initial discovery to final commit, the question of "did this actually move the needle" was always in the back of my mind. I was confident in the direction, but a few things stood out as areas for improvement.
retro.p2: This was also my first major feature at HubSpot, and navigating a larger stakeholder audience while still getting up to speed came with its own challenges. In hindsight, I would have built more time into the timeline to bring stakeholders in earlier rather than mid-flight. In my experience, projects with a broad audience benefit from a bit more upfront discovery. Each project like this teaches me something new about how to handle them better.
retro.p3: Even with some lumps and bumps, I was still happy with how things ended with the minor exception of not being able to see some of the future plans I had cooked up through to production when they were ready. Most importantly, our customers were happy and appreciative of the changes we delivered and also excited for many of the forward-looking things we showed off during our interviews.

bill-pay.title: Improving the most core data management flow in HubSpot's CRM to save admins time, money, and [data] sanity

intro.p1: Solving customer pain points, driving adoption, and reducing internal and external overhead costs by rethinking the way customers create and edit their custom data properties.

context.title: Context.
context.p1: HubSpot's CRM is the core of their product and where customers first build out their HubSpot experience. This made it critical to nail onboarding and data integration from the start.
context.p2: The challenge was offering a robust data creation and management experience that still felt nimble across customers of all sizes. Internal and external feedback told us the existing framework was rigid, redundant, and limited — the opposite of the original goal. It forced customers of all sizes into a single mold and wasn't meeting their needs.

problem.title: The problem.
problem.p1: A spike in customer support tickets around property management, upcoming internal feature kick-offs, and an opportunity to adopt new design standards from the core product team gave us the perfect moment to rethink and rebuild this workflow from the ground up.
problem.p2: This didn't have to be a large undertaking and I could have taken a more incremental approach with smaller wins over time, but we decided to aim higher, because the potential upside for our customers was worth the risk.

challenges.title: Challenges.
challenges.p1a: The wizard pattern was well-established with customers, even if disliked
challenges.p1b: Even with strong negative sentiment in interviews and surveys, we risked running into usability biases like "it just works" or "I don't like change" mentalities that could drive churn. This same resistance is likely why some customers resorted to building their own API-first solutions rather than adopting a WYSIWYG experience that should have been easier to use.
challenges.p2a: As a precaution, scope needed to be pared down more than anticipated
challenges.p2b: This flow generated the building blocks that supported all other features and flows in the CRM for any customer, so if care wasn't taken, it could've had a catastrophic ripple effect.
challenges.p3a: Getting other teams to adopt a new component proved challenging
challenges.p3b: Several other product teams drove traffic to our page or had built their own features pushing property data to our tables. In a product this complex, consistency mattered and deviations weren't ideal. I worked closely with each team to negotiate, adapt our solution to their needs, and build their confidence in adopting our component over their own.
challenges.p4a: Admins are busy and have lives and we should not be encroaching on them
challenges.p4b: Everyone only has a limited amount of time per day to do any number of things, so why would they want to spend hours (or days) doing a task. If the new flow didn't reduce time on task, it wouldn't have been worth releasing until it did.

solving.title: Problem-solving.
solving.p1: After several major iteration rounds and feedback, I went down two paths: a quick creation component (a stripped-down, deployable flow for more common property types) and advanced property management (a richer experience designed for admins).
solving.p2: We took this approach for two reasons: consistency and role-appropriate experience. Guardrails keep property creation uniform across the CRM, while the two-path framework gives admins full control and gives marketers and downstream teams something faster and more focused.
solving.p3: User testing, beta feedback, and input from our stakeholders shaped the final production spec. I worked with a content design partner to polish the details before handing it off to engineering and shifting into QA.

impact.title: Impact.
impact.p1: After a two-week closed beta and a month-long open beta reaching roughly 15% of Pro+ tier customers, we shipped to production in mid-March to a warm reception on r/HubSpot and our customer forums. Post-release surveys and interviews were promising, with CSAT improving and customer sentiment no longer including words like "archaic," "redundant," or "painful."
impact.p2: In the first month after launch, support volume dropped more than 20% week-over-week, climbing to ~35% in the weeks that followed.
impact.p3: Being that this was my first release where I discovered, pitched, prioritized, iterated, and executed end-to-end in my time there, I was really pleased with the framework delivered and the roadmap that was planned for the future.

retro.title: Retro.
retro.p1: No project is without turbulence, and this one was no exception. A few things stood out as areas for growth.
retro.p2: Communication is a force multiplier at the senior IC level. I had autonomy, but autonomy can breed tunnel vision. Midway through, I recalibrated and tightened how I communicated decisions and added more polish to written updates. It kept the team aligned and the project on track.
retro.p3: HubSpot's concurrent brand and product refresh left my design systems partners largely unavailable, which added unplanned time to the timeline. I adapted by scaling back some decisions where I could, and it didn't hurt the outcome.
retro.p4: Stakeholder management was the biggest learning. This was my first large-scale feature at HubSpot, and I would have mapped the stakeholder landscape earlier in the process. Mid-flight is never the right time to be expanding your audience. It's a lesson I carried into every project from then on.
retro.p5: Overall, I was proud of where it landed, but with the one caveat that some forward-looking ideas I had scoped didn't make it to production before I moved on.
